title: AI Needs Public Feedback at Scale Before It’s Too Late | NOEMA
gist: Noema's editor-in-chief synthesizes two of the magazine's essays — Macario Schettino's historical pattern that every communications disruption is eventually tamed by a maturer form of the same technology, and Hélène Landemore's argument that the chatbot install base (roughly a billion monthly users each at OpenAI, Google and Meta) is already the largest two-way deliberative channel in history — into a direct, named demand that Amodei, Altman and Zuckerberg fund a three-tier global consultation to write democratically sourced AI constitutions. The piece is mostly curation rather than original argument, and its operative content is a labs-should-self-govern playbook backed by cited pilot results, not a call for state regulation.

insights.claim: Every prior communication-driven disruption — printing press, mass newspapers, radio, TV — was eventually tamed by a maturer form of the same technology that caused it, implying social media's chaos gets resolved by AI-shaped social media rather than by abandoning platforms.
insights.speaker: Macario Schettino
insights.so_what: Frames platform-plus-AI incumbents as the eventual infrastructure of social order rather than a doomed category, arguing against a thesis that regulation kills the attention-platform business model.
insights.quote: In each case, what initially fragmented the public sphere is what, in its maturer form, eventually rebuilt it.
insights.locator: The printing press tore the medieval frame apart

insights.claim: The historical settlement timelines for communication disruptions are measured in generations, not quarters: the Reformation took 131 years to reach the Peace of Westphalia, and the mass-media transition produced two world wars and a Cold War before the postwar order stabilized.
insights.speaker: Macario Schettino
insights.so_what: Sets expectations that AI-era governance normalization is a multi-decade regime, so any investment thesis premised on near-term regulatory clarity is mispriced on duration.
insights.quote: “The Reformation required 131 years to settle into the Peace of Westphalia. The Enlightenment needed longer,”
insights.locator: Even though we live in accelerated times

insights.claim: We are currently in the chaotic phase of the social-media transition, historically analogous to the Wars of Religion or the demagogue's radio, meaning the interaction of AI with social platforms is more likely to deepen disorder before it tames it.
insights.speaker: NATHAN GARDELS
insights.so_what: Implies a worsening-before-better path for information-integrity risk, elevating near-term political and content-moderation tail risk for platform operators.
insights.quote: The interaction of AI with social platforms could deepen the current chaos, but it is also the most plausible candidate to eventually tame the disorder.
insights.locator: If the pattern holds, the disruption caused by social media

themes.theme: Chatbot Install Base as Deliberative Infrastructure

insights.claim: OpenAI reported 900 million weekly active ChatGPT users in February and crossed a billion monthly users in June, while Google's Gemini went from 400 million to more than 900 million monthly active users on a similar timeline and Meta AI reported a billion monthly users.
insights.speaker: Hélène Landemore
insights.so_what: Three-way parity near the billion-user mark means consumer AI distribution is no longer OpenAI's moat; differentiation has to come from monetization or vertical depth, not reach.
insights.quote: OpenAI reported 900 million weekly active ChatGPT users in February and crossed a billion monthly users in June.
insights.locator: As Hélène Landemore writes in Noema

insights.claim: No government, broadcaster or international body has ever had standing two-way contact with as large a portion of humanity as today's frontier AI companies, making the labs — not elected leaders — the parties best positioned to facilitate a global deliberation on AI.
insights.speaker: Hélène Landemore
insights.so_what: Argues for private-sector-led legitimacy processes as a substitute for state regulation, a framing that favors incumbent labs shaping their own governance terms.
insights.quote: Right now, the people best placed to actually facilitate a global deliberation on AI may not be elected leaders and heads of governments, but the heads of the companies building this technology.
insights.locator: No government, broadcaster or international body

insights.claim: Because the general public's information is what algorithms convert into future productive capacity, the public has a claim on how that capacity is ultimately used — an ownership-style argument for consent over training data.
insights.speaker: NATHAN GARDELS
insights.so_what: This is the intellectual scaffolding for data-rights and compensation claims against model builders; watch it migrate into litigation and licensing demands.
insights.quote: Since it is the general public whose information is being transformed by algorithms into the productive capacity of the future, reaching social consensus means they must have a say in its ultimate use.
insights.locator: Infrastructure Already Exists

insights.claim: An Economist investigation comparing the apparent values of 25 frontier AI models to the World Values Survey found the models often hold values more extreme than the average respondent across the 88 countries surveyed — in some cases more secular or more individualist than any society on Earth.
insights.speaker: Hélène Landemore
insights.so_what: Quantified cultural skew is an emerging compliance and localization risk for model deployment in non-Western markets, and a wedge for sovereign-AI competitors.
insights.quote: the models often hold values more extreme than the average respondent in the 88 countries surveyed by the WVS — in some cases more secular or more individualist than any society on Earth
insights.locator: Landemore notes a recent investigation by The Economist

insights.claim: Frontier models compress the world's moral diversity, so running humanity's input through them unchecked would make the supposedly global constitutional baseline the baseline of one narrow cultural corner.
insights.speaker: Hélène Landemore
insights.so_what: Undercuts the credibility of any lab-run 'global' values exercise conducted purely through its own model — audit trails and human layers become the differentiator.
insights.quote: If we ran humanity’s input through such models unchecked, the ‘global’ constitutional baseline would risk becoming that of one narrow cultural corner.
insights.locator: Landemore notes a recent investigation by The Economist

insights.claim: The RLHF corrective that technologists apply to model hallucinations and eclipsed information should be extended to society itself, inviting public deliberation into what has been the exclusive domain of Big Tech elites and their algorithmic agents.
insights.speaker: NATHAN GARDELS
insights.so_what: A memorable analogy — 'RLHF for governance' — that could become the shorthand policymakers use to demand participatory alignment processes.
insights.quote: As with AI processes in general, hallucinations, false impressions and eclipsed information in frontier models need what technologists call “reinforcement learning from human feedback” as a corrective.
insights.locator: As with AI processes in general, hallucinations

insights.claim: The proposed design layers a multi-year human deliberative process on top of fast LLM-mediated consultations, with each of three tiers adding back what speed alone lacks: an independent accountability record and a wider range of minds.
insights.speaker: Hélène Landemore
insights.so_what: A concrete, staged blueprint that a lab or foundation could fund tomorrow — the kind of process spec that tends to get cited once mandatory AI-governance standards are drafted.
insights.quote: The real issue is thus one of representativeness and accountability
insights.locator: “The real issue is thus one of representativeness

insights.claim: Tier one could produce an interim global draft within months and should deliberately be broken out by region rather than flattened into a single average, surfacing genuine divergence such as a Western emphasis on individual data privacy and precautionary restriction versus a data-sovereignty and development-first framing more common in Africa and India.
insights.speaker: Hélène Landemore
insights.so_what: Names the actual fault line in global AI rulemaking — precaution versus development — which is the axis to watch for divergent regional compliance regimes and market access costs.
insights.locator: The first tier, an LLM-mediated global consultation

insights.claim: Tier two — real-time online global deliberation among humans mediated by AI facilitators — is designed to test and sometimes replace the recommendations that emerged from LLM-aggregated input, treating machine output as a draft to be corrected rather than a result.
insights.speaker: Hélène Landemore
insights.so_what: Creates demand for a new tooling category: AI facilitation and deliberation platforms, an underbuilt niche relative to the assistant market.
insights.locator: The second tier would be more logistically demanding

insights.claim: Tier three would run local and national citizens' assemblies in every country and region, ideally combined with referenda, feeding into a concluding global citizens' assembly that could ratify, amend or supersede earlier drafts — explicitly engineered so that a short timeline still leaves a usable floor in place.
insights.speaker: Hélène Landemore
insights.so_what: The fail-safe structure is the tell: the author is hedging against a short AGI timeline, which is itself a signal about how the deliberation community is pricing capability risk.
insights.quote: If the clock turns out to be as short as feared, we would not be left with nothing.
insights.locator: The third tier would reach deeper still

themes.theme: Lab Pilots as Existing Proof of Concept

insights.claim: In 2023 Anthropic and the Collective Intelligence Project sourced constitutional principles from roughly 1,000 ordinary Americans and found that a model trained on those principles produced less biased outputs in some areas than the standard internally authored model — evidence that public input improves model quality, not just legitimacy.
insights.speaker: Hélène Landemore
insights.so_what: If participatory alignment measurably reduces bias, it becomes a product-performance argument rather than a PR expense — a cheaper path to enterprise trust than adversarial red-teaming alone.
insights.quote: This is evidence that public input doesn’t just confer legitimacy, it can make a model better.
insights.locator: To Dario Amodei, CEO of Anthropic

insights.claim: In 2025 Anthropic used an AI interviewer to survey nearly 81,000 Claude users across 159 countries and 70 languages in a single week, demonstrating that model-mediated global consultation already scales operationally.
insights.speaker: Hélène Landemore
insights.so_what: Concrete throughput benchmark: 81,000 respondents in 159 countries in one week is the cost floor competitors will be measured against for any consultation claim.
insights.quote: Anthropic used an AI interviewer to ask nearly 81,000 Claude users across 159 countries and 70 languages in a single week how they use AI
insights.locator: In 2025, Anthropic used an AI interviewer

insights.claim: Anthropic's new Claude Constitution published in January was written the same way its predecessor was — by a small internal team with model input and a handful of outside experts, but not the tens of millions of users the model talks to — which the author frames as a failure of will rather than capability.
insights.speaker: Hélène Landemore
insights.so_what: A specific, dated criticism of the most safety-branded lab; the gap between stated values and process is the sort of thing that becomes an attack surface in procurement and policy hearings.
insights.quote: What’s missing isn’t proof of concept. It’s the will to use it.
insights.locator: In January, Anthropic published a new “Constitution”

insights.claim: OpenAI's 2023 Democratic Inputs to AI program funded 10 teams selected from nearly 1,000 applicants to prototype public-input mechanisms, but never amounted to anything close to what OpenAI's reach could support.
insights.speaker: Hélène Landemore
insights.so_what: A named advisor calling out an abandoned OpenAI governance initiative signals eroding goodwill among the academic legitimacy community OpenAI once recruited.
insights.quote: Finish what you started, at the scale this moment demands, with resources commensurate with what you yourself keep saying is at stake.
insights.locator: To Sam Altman, CEO of OpenAI

insights.claim: Meta's 2022 Community Forum on Cyberbullying in the Metaverse, run with Stanford's Deliberative Democracy Lab and the Behavioral Insights Team, gathered small-group online deliberations from nearly 6,500 people across 32 countries, and its 2023 and 2024 forums on generative AI each drew more than 1,000 participants across the West and Global South on chatbot transparency, cultural sensitivities and data retention.
insights.speaker: Hélène Landemore
insights.so_what: Meta already owns the largest working template for tier-two deliberation; the ask is to convert one-off sentiment pilots into a standing institution at billion-user scale.
insights.quote: not as a couple of one-off pilots measuring sentiment, but as a standing global institution that democracies have never had the tools to build
insights.locator: To Mark Zuckerberg, CEO of Meta

themes.theme: Governance Signals and the State Capacity Gap

insights.claim: Anthropic's new chief global affairs officer Tino Cuéllar, a former California Supreme Court justice, opened by saying democracies must set the terms on which the technology advances — and he was a key figure in designing Engaged California.
insights.speaker: Tino Cuéllar
insights.so_what: A personnel signal that Anthropic is building deliberative-governance capability in-house; watch for Anthropic to lead on participatory alignment as a regulatory differentiator.
insights.quote: “democracies must set the terms on which this technology advances.”
insights.locator: It is a good sign that Tino Cuéllar

insights.claim: The closing appeal extends to tech leaders in the U.S., China and beyond on the explicit premise that no government is moving fast enough, or has the will or standing, to write global and local AI constitutions alone.
insights.speaker: Hélène Landemore
insights.so_what: The expectation of state failure on AI rulemaking implies private standards-setting fills the vacuum — first movers get to define the norms their competitors are measured against.
insights.quote: Help bring democratically written global and local constitutions on AI into being, because right now no government is moving fast enough, or has the will or standing, to do it alone.
insights.locator: To every other tech leader in the U.S., China and beyond
